name: Battalion Strength
description: There are $$$n$$$ officers in the Army of Byteland. Each officer has some power associated with him. The power of the $$$i$$$-th officer is denoted by $$$p_{i}$$$. As the war is fast approaching, the General would like to know the strength of the army. The strength of an army is calculated in a strange way in Byteland. The General selects a random subset of officers from these $$$n$$$ officers and calls this subset a battalion.(All $$$2^n$$$ subsets of the $$$n$$$ officers can be chosen equally likely, including empty subset and the subset of all officers). The strength of a battalion is calculated in the following way: Let the powers of the chosen officers be $$$a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}$$$, where $$$a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_k$$$. The strength of this battalion is equal to $$$a_1a_2 + a_2a_3 + \dots + a_{k-1}a_k$$$. (If the size of Battalion is $$$\leq 1$$$, then the strength of this battalion is $$$0$$$). The strength of the army is equal to the expected value of the strength of the battalion. As the war is really long, the powers of officers may change. Precisely, there will be $$$q$$$ changes. Each one of the form $$$i$$$ $$$x$$$ indicating that $$$p_{i}$$$ is changed to $$$x$$$. You need to find the strength of the army initially and after each of these $$$q$$$ updates. Note that the changes are permanent. The strength should be found by modulo $$$10^{9}+7$$$. Formally, let $$$M=10^{9}+7$$$. It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $$$p/q$$$, where $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ are integers and $$$q\not\equiv 0 \bmod M$$$). Output the integer equal to $$$p\cdot q^{-1} \bmod M$$$. In other words, output such an integer $$$x$$$ that $$$0 \leq x \lt M$$$ and $$$x ⋅ q \equiv p \bmod M$$$).
input_specification: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 3⋅10^{5}$$$)  — the number of officers in Byteland's Army. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n}$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_{i} \leq 10^{9}$$$). The third line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \leq q \leq 3⋅10^{5}$$$)  — the number of updates. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$i$$$ and $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \leq i \leq n$$$, $$$ 1 \leq x \leq 10^{9}$$$), indicating that $$$p_{i}$$$ is updated to $$$x$$$ .
output_specification: In the first line output the initial strength of the army. In $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$q$$$ lines, output the strength of the army after $$$i$$$-th update.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1316F — Battalion Strength [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
